blocks.text: [III, 103] which birds differ greatly. For the otus is a nocturnal bird, ὅμοιος ταῖς γλαυξὶ, καὶ περὶ τὰ ὦτα πτερύγια ἔχων, ἔνιοι δὲ αὐτὸν νυκτικόρακα καλοῦσιν [homoios tais glauxi, kai peri ta ōta pterygia echōn, enioi de auton nyktikoraka kalousin], like the little owl, having little feathers around its ears, which is why it is called otus): some call it the night raven. But the otis, called tarda by others, is a species of wild fowl, in Arabic حباري [ḥubārá] hubara, which has already been treated ^{d)}. And this bird is indeed melancholy; hence the Arabs say كمد من الحباري [kamad min al-ḥubārá] more melancholy than the otis for 'extremely melancholy'; yet it is not irascible. Gesner describes it as very timid and faint-hearted, so that it dies even if only slightly wounded. Such great faint-heartedness can hardly coexist with irascibility, for anger is the whetstone of courage. Therefore I cannot at all understand why the Jews would have the anapha be the otis, especially since it is a species of fowl, and all species of fowl are held to be clean.

To pursue the rest in the same way would be lengthy and of little use. So we shall add only two points, less obvious: why for anapha the Greeks, whom Jerome follows, have χαραδριὸν [charadrion], and the printed Arabic has ببغا [babghā] or ببغاة [babghāh], parrot. The charadrius, as is well known, got its name from αἱ χαράδραι [hai charadrai], that is, clefts near rivers and torrents, in which this bird nests. Hence the Philosopher, History, book 9, chapter 11: Τὰς δὲ οἰκήσεις οἱ μὲν περὶ τὰς χαράδρας, οἱ δὲ χηραμοὺς ποιοῦνται, καὶ πέτρας, οἷον ὁ καλούμενος χαραδριός [Tas de oikēseis hoi men peri tas charadras, hoi de chēramous poiountai, kai petras, hoion ho kaloumenos charadrios]. Gaza rendered this thus: Others (birds) inhabit rugged places, rocks and caves, like the one we call charadrius from the steep beds of torrents, as if you were to say cleft-dweller. And the Scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds: Ὠνοματοπεποίηται τὸ ὄρνεον παρὰ τὸ ἐν ταῖς χαράδραις διατρίβειν [Ōnomatopepoiētai to orneon para to en tais charadrais diatribein]. That bird is so called because it lives in clefts along river banks. Accordingly, when in the Comic poet the birds were building the city of Nephelococcygia in the clouds,
Ὕδωρ ἐφόρουν κάτωθεν ἐς τὸν ἀέρα Οἱ χαραδριοὶ, καὶ τ᾽ ἄλλα ποτάμι᾽ ὄρνεα, [Hydōr ephoroun katōthen es ton aera / Hoi charadrioi, kai t' alla potami' ornea,]

The charadrii and the other river birds carried water from below into the air. Now, to this name charadrius there corresponds not אנפה anapha but אגפה agapha, which is how we conjecture the Greek translators read it, with Nun and Gimel interchanged, letters which are very similar. For אגף agaph in a bird is the wing, in a man the arm, in a river or channel the bank. As in Bava Bathra ch. 6, fol. 99b: ואמה מכאן ואמה מכאן לאגפיה, And a cubit on this side and a cubit on that side, at its banks. Hence Baal Aruch: פירוש אגפיה גדותיה כדכתיב והירדן מלא על כל גדותיו אגפיים ראשונים בעופות ושניים באדם ושלשים בנהר ופתרון אחד להם. The sense is that the word אגפיה is the same as גרותיה, its banks; as when in Ios. III, 15 [col. 341]

[III, 104] the river Jordan is read to have overflowed all its banks. And that אגפיים is used first of birds for wings; second of man for arms; third of a river for banks; yet in such a way that by analogy these three mean the same thing, because banks are to a river what wings are to a bird and arms to a man, that is, equally on either side. Since, therefore, the word אגף agaph was in use among the Jews for a river bank at the time when the Greek translators published their version, they thought that a bird accustomed to nest on river banks, that is, the charadrius, was called from it אגפה agapha, or rather agappa ^{(2)}.
